Malevolent means having a deep, active desire to cause harm, pain, or suffering to others. A malevolent person doesn't just do harmful things by accident or out of anger in the moment — they want others to suffer. The desire itself is the heart of the word.

Think of it this way: if someone accidentally bumps into you and spills your coffee, that's not malevolent. If someone knocks your coffee over on purpose because they want your day to be ruined, and they feel pleasure doing it, that is malevolent. The key is the deliberate, deep-seated wish for harm.

Malevolent is a heavy, serious word. It sits at the darker end of the spectrum of "wanting bad things for others." You wouldn't use it to describe someone who was simply rude to you or cut you off in traffic. It implies something darker, colder, and more intentional — almost like evil is baked into a person's character or attitude.

Imagine a villain in a story who doesn't just want to win — they want the hero to suffer. They enjoy watching others in pain. That is a malevolent character. The word carries a sense of something sinister and deeply felt, not just a passing bad mood.
What Can Be Described as Malevolent?

This is where the word becomes very useful, because it isn't limited to just people.

A person can be malevolent — a malevolent ruler who takes pleasure in punishing citizens for no reason.

A look or expression can be malevolent — he gave her a slow, malevolent smile that made her feel unsafe.

A plan or intention can be malevolent — the scheme was entirely malevolent in design, meant only to destroy his rival's reputation.

A force or presence can be malevolent — in horror and fantasy, you'll often read about a malevolent spirit or a malevolent entity haunting a place. Here the word perfectly captures something that intends evil, not just something dangerous by nature (like a storm).

The common thread across all these uses: intention and desire to harm are present.
Malevolent vs. Words That Feel Similar

Understanding what makes a word different from its neighbors is one of the best ways to truly own it.

Malevolent vs. Mean: "Mean" is a mild, everyday word for unkindness. Someone who teases their little sibling is being mean. Calling that same person malevolent would be a dramatic overstatement. Malevolent is reserved for something genuinely dark.

Malevolent vs. Hostile: Hostile means unfriendly, aggressive, or openly opposed to someone. A hostile crowd boos a speaker. But hostile doesn't necessarily mean they wish deep harm — they might just want that person gone. Malevolent goes deeper; it implies a desire to see real suffering.

Malevolent vs. Wicked: Wicked usually describes actions or behaviour that goes against moral standards — a wicked deed, a wicked scheme. Malevolent, on the other hand, focuses more on the inner desire or disposition — it's about what someone wants deep inside.

Malevolent vs. Malicious: These two are the closest pair and are often used interchangeably. Both involve intent to harm. The subtle difference is that malicious tends to focus on specific harmful acts or intentions (he sent a malicious email to destroy her career), while malevolent often describes a broader, more pervasive, almost character-level quality of wishing harm (he was a malevolent presence in the office, slowly poisoning every relationship). Malevolent also fits supernatural or abstract descriptions more naturally.

The antonym of malevolent is benevolent. A benevolent person genuinely wants good things for others — they are kind, generous, and wish well for those around them. Knowing this pair makes both words stick far better in your mind. Wherever you see mal-, think "bad/evil." Wherever you see bene-, think "good/well."

Since you'll encounter this word's family in your reading and writing, here are the other forms:

Malevolence (noun) — the quality or state of being malevolent. "There was a cold malevolence in his eyes that everyone in the room could feel."

Malevolently (adverb) — in a malevolent way. "She stared at him malevolently as he walked away."

If you had to carry one sentence in your mind forever to remember what malevolent means, let it be this:

A malevolent person doesn't just do harm — they want to, they intend to, and on some level, they enjoy it.

It is a word for describing evil that is deliberate, deep, and conscious — whether in a real person's character, a supernatural force, or a cold, threatening expression. Use it when "mean" or "hostile" simply aren't dark enough, and when the desire to cause suffering is clearly at the centre of what you're describing.
